title: Lifelong on-robot learning that retains and composes physical skills

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a deployed robot that keeps building its physical skill repertoire through use. It learns genuinely new tasks from limited instruction or corrections, retains the tasks it learned earlier, and combines those skills to complete a new job in a different environment. The central capability is cumulative learning: teaching the next procedure should expand what the robot can do without requiring it to relearn its previous procedures.

Conceptual synthesis: acquisition, retention and composition must work together on the physical robot. A system that already performs an unfamiliar task using a frozen policy demonstrates generalization; a system that updates its capabilities through a sequence of new tasks demonstrates learning. Either can support the other, but successful execution alone does not establish that new knowledge was acquired or that earlier skills survived the update.

Replay of stored experience can be part of sequential learning. Sequential acquisition means that new tasks arrive over time; it does not require erasing access to all previous experience. Simultaneous multi-task training does not itself test acquisition through a task stream, whereas replay can mitigate forgetting within such a stream. Prohibiting replay of original demonstrations is therefore an additional proposed constraint on this innovation, rather than its definition.

Proposed stricter extensions include learning a skill from a single demonstration and transferring that newly acquired skill to another robot body without further training. These remain extensions of the same learning capability. They add substantial requirements beyond retaining and composing skills on one body, and success on a second robot would establish transfer to that tested embodiment rather than to arbitrary bodies.

significance.text: The revolutionary consequence would be a change in the marginal cost of teaching physical work. If a deployed robot could acquire a new procedure from a small number of corrections while preserving its existing competence, some additional data collection and retraining could become ordinary on-the-job instruction. Retention would protect previous teaching effort, while composition would let learned skills contribute to jobs that were never demonstrated as complete sequences. Existing research on knowledge preservation, reuse and language coaching supports this technical rationale without demonstrating the full capability.

Conditional impact synthesis: warehouses, kitchens and laboratories could benefit when their procedures change more often than a fixed training campaign can economically accommodate. The direct benefit would apply within the robot's demonstrated operating range. Broad replacement of collection campaigns would additionally require adequate perception, dexterity, reliability and safety; efficient learning alone would not supply those capabilities or establish that deployment is economical.

The analogy to updating a software model has an important physical limit. A robot must collect experience through actions that can damage objects, interrupt work or endanger people. Lifelong learning must therefore reconcile improvement with safe deployment, rather than merely make model updates inexpensive. The accessible robotics roadmap identifies lifelong learning and safe deployment as long-term challenges, but does not establish a solution to their combination.

Conceptual synthesis: the practical value depends on genuinely new tasks continuing to arise. If a frozen policy eventually covered every relevant job, the need for further learning in that setting would diminish. Conversely, transferring a known skill between bodies can expand deployment without showing cumulative learning: embodiment transfer alone does not establish that the robot can acquire a new task sequence and retain its earlier skills.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing integrated capability is efficient sequential acquisition on the deployed robot, measured preservation of earlier skills, and reliable reuse in a new setting. Catastrophic forgetting creates a central tension: changes that help the newest task can degrade earlier behavior. Replay-based lifelong methods demonstrate ways to address this tension, but their success in bounded task streams does not establish the proposed combination under limited physical instruction.

Engineering synthesis: instruction efficiency must be measured against the full cost of learning. A small correction count could conceal lengthy corrections, extensive autonomous exploration, repeated resets or substantial computation. The robot would need to turn sparse feedback into useful updates while keeping these costs and physical risks within declared limits. It would also need to preserve competent behavior during learning, not merely recover it after a later retraining campaign.

Reliable composition requires more than remembering isolated motor routines. Skills must remain usable when objects, spatial relationships and preceding actions change. LEGION demonstrates bounded reuse, including table-cleaning combinations, but its structured environments, predefined task setups and AprilTag-based perception leave substantial distance to composition in an unfamiliar room with less engineered perception.

Establishing that a task is genuinely new is also difficult for broadly pretrained robots. The π0.7 paper acknowledges that related behaviors may exist elsewhere in its large training dataset. A convincing learning claim therefore needs a declared prior and an audit of task-specific exposure, so that retrieval or recombination of existing competence is not mistaken for acquisition from the new instruction.

Single-demonstration acquisition and transfer without retraining across different bodies introduce further barriers. The supplied reports show bounded transfer or adaptation, including simulated manipulator swaps, zero-shot transfer of selected skills and adaptation to new bi-arm systems using additional examples. They do not establish the combined single-demonstration, arbitrary-body target. Engineering synthesis: differences in reach, workspace, sensing and action interfaces require explicit embodiment boundaries; some tasks may be physically infeasible on a target body.

current_state.text: Yuan Meng and colleagues published “Preserving and combining knowledge in robotic lifelong reinforcement learning” in Nature Machine Intelligence on 5 February 2025. Their LEGION system learns a sequence of ten predefined manipulation tasks in simulation, using one million training steps per task. Retention is evaluated principally during simulation training within a bounded family that includes reach, push, faucet, button and window variants. This is evidence for sequential knowledge preservation and reuse, but it does not demonstrate learning new physical tasks from tens of on-robot corrections.

After simulation training, the authors deploy the trained model on a real KUKA manipulator with its parameters frozen, executing individual tasks and combinations such as cleaning a table. The physical demonstration therefore shows deployment and skill reuse rather than sequential on-robot acquisition. The framework uses structured environments, predefined task setups and AprilTags for perception. Its soft actor-critic policy retains replay, and the study also investigates intermittent replay in sequential learning, including a buffer holding only three tasks.

LEGION's supplement reports bounded heterogeneous-embodiment experiments, including swapping simulated KUKA and Sawyer manipulators so that each executes tasks originally trained on the other without fine-tuning, subject to workspace constraints. This is relevant evidence for transfer, although it is much narrower than immediate transfer to arbitrary physical bodies. The supplied review bases this finding on supplementary prose; videos and snapshots were not independently inspected. The main article's complete HTML supports its central findings despite extraction problems in a separate PDF, and a nearly textless additional supplement does not support further conclusions.

Aude Billard and colleagues' “A roadmap for AI in robotics,” published on 19 June 2025 in Nature Machine Intelligence 7, pages 818–824, identifies lifelong learning and safe deployment as long-term challenges. Its accessible abstract also discusses algorithms that transfer across robotic platforms as a research objective. This is a community roadmap rather than an experimental demonstration. Only the abstract and subscription preview were available to the supplied review, so detailed conclusions cannot be attributed to the inaccessible full text or figures.

In its 30 July 2026 report, DeepMind states that Gemini Robotics On-Device 2 can adapt to new bi-arm embodiments in a few hours, typically using fewer than 200 examples. These are developer-reported adaptation figures, not independently verified performance in the supplied material. They describe rapid adaptation with additional training rather than single-demonstration acquisition or transfer without retraining to arbitrary bodies. The embedded videos were not inspected in the supplied review.

The April 2026 π0.7 arXiv preprint reports zero-shot cross-embodiment transfer of selected dexterous skills, including towel and shirt folding on a bimanual UR5e system for which the authors report collecting no laundry-folding data. It also describes training a high-level policy from language-coached episodes to perform new, longer-horizon tasks. Those coaching results are a relevant learning component and should not be omitted by describing the work solely as batch training. However, the text inspected in the supplied review does not report sequential on-robot acquisition paired with an earlier-task retention test. The retained extraction ends during Appendix A-G, so this is a bounded conclusion about the available text, not an exhaustive absence claim.

Evidence synthesis as of 1 November 2026: the supplied studies document components of the proposed innovation, but do not establish its full combination of limited-instruction physical acquisition, retention and composition in a new environment. No freshness search was supplied to establish exhaustive coverage through that date. Consequently, these materials cannot settle whether another result elsewhere has met the target; limitations in coverage or extraction are not evidence that a reported result is false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: start one physical robot from a declared model and training history, then teach it a prespecified sequence of real tasks whose task-specific training data were excluded from that prior. Declare the task count, ordering, novelty checks and operating conditions before testing. Establish baseline performance before instruction so that existing competence can be distinguished from learning. These are proposed evaluation requirements, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Prespecified prior-excluded real-task sequence learned on one robot after baseline

completion_criteria.text: Proposed learning budget: allow a prespecified number in the tens of on-robot corrections per task. Report correction duration and content, total physical interaction, autonomous exploration, resets, human assistance, computation and elapsed learning time. This would make the intended advantage over large demonstration-collection campaigns assessable without treating correction count as a complete measure of effort.
completion_criteria.label: Tens of on-robot corrections per task with full resource costs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed retention test: measure every earlier task after subsequent learning and again at the end, without intervening retraining on the tested task. Prespecify task-success definitions, acceptable retention loss, trial counts and uncertainty reporting. Report both individual-task results and aggregates so that strong performance on recent tasks cannot conceal forgetting of early ones. The success and retention thresholds remain choices for the proposed demonstration.
completion_criteria.label: Every earlier task retested without retraining, individually and in aggregate

completion_criteria.text: Proposed composition and memory test: after the learning sequence, require a new multi-step job in a new room that combines acquired skills without supplying a complete demonstration of that job. Declare any room setup, perception aids and adaptation allowed. Preserve the candidate's stricter prohibition on offline replay of original demonstrations, while explicitly declaring permitted memory, other replay mechanisms and prior data access. That prohibition tests an additional constraint; it does not define sequential learning.
completion_criteria.label: Multi-step new-room composition without full demonstration or offline original-demo replay

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: repeat learning runs with declared task orders and report failures, interventions, safety events and performance variation. Provide sufficient training, evaluation and interaction records for independent replication where feasible. State the tested objects, environments, hardware and risk limits. Finite trials can establish demonstrated breadth and reliability within those boundaries, not literal lifelong retention or universal task competence.
completion_criteria.label: Repeated declared-order runs with replication records and stated boundaries

completion_criteria.text: Proposed stricter extension: separately test acquisition from a single demonstration, then execute the newly learned skill on a second, different robot without further training. Declare any calibration, controller changes or embodiment-specific configuration. Success would establish transfer to that tested body. A stronger cross-embodiment claim would require a broader, explicitly bounded range of bodies and physically feasible tasks; no finite second-robot test establishes arbitrary-body transfer.
completion_criteria.label: Single-demonstration transfer to one different robot without further training

related_concepts.text: Roster-based conceptual comparison: ROB-01, “Reliable instruction-following physical work in unfamiliar everyday environments,” overlaps in generalization and deployment. Its title permits success through a frozen policy, whereas ROB-09 specifically requires accumulating new skills while retaining earlier ones. A robot could satisfy aspects of either capability without satisfying the other. Only ROB-01's title is supplied, so its complete catalog scope cannot be independently reconciled here.

Roster-based conceptual comparison: ROB-02, “Autonomous dexterous tool use and in-hand manipulation at human reliability,” concerns the quality and reliability of manipulation. ROB-07, “Predictive contact mechanics that plans real manipulation,” concerns predicting physical interactions for planning. Both could support learning more demanding skills, but dexterity or accurate contact prediction alone does not demonstrate sequential retention and composition. ROB-09 could also be demonstrated initially on tasks with modest dexterity demands.

Roster-based conceptual comparison: ROB-03, “An artificial muscle that can serve as the main actuator of a useful robot,” concerns actuation hardware. ROB-05, “Load-bearing robotic matter that reforms into working machines,” concerns reconfigurable physical structure. Such technologies could provide bodies on which learning operates and make embodiment adaptation especially relevant, but neither hardware capability establishes lifelong learning. ROB-09 does not require either technology.

Roster-based conceptual comparison: ROB-04, “Closed-loop robotic self-reproduction from feedstock,” and ROB-08, “Robot collectives that build functional structures from bulk material,” concern production and construction outcomes. Retained and composable skills could help robots adapt those processes to changing conditions, but either outcome could potentially rely on fixed procedures. ROB-09 does not require self-reproduction or collective construction, and it does not subsume them.

Roster-based conceptual comparison: ROB-06, “Untethered intervention at a target inside the living human body,” and ROB-10, “Completion of full surgical procedures on living patients,” concern specific medical capabilities and operating conditions. Lifelong learning could be relevant to adaptation in such systems, but success on ordinary manipulation tasks would establish neither medical capability. Conversely, a fixed medical system could achieve its specified procedure without accumulating new skills during deployment. These entries remain distinct.

change_log.reason: The research and review support a coherent innovation; limitations in particular supporting claims do not justify removing or splitting it.

change_log.change: Corrected the assertion that replay leaves the sequential-learning setting.
change_log.reason: LEGION and its replay baselines learn sequential task streams. Excluding original-demonstration replay is retained as an additional proposed constraint.

change_log.change: Separated LEGION's simulation learning from its frozen-parameter KUKA deployment and retained its quantitative training scope.
change_log.reason: Ten sequential tasks and one million training steps per task do not constitute limited-correction sequential learning on the physical robot.

change_log.change: Added bounded simulated embodiment-transfer results and π0.7's language-coaching results.
change_log.reason: These relevant components were omitted or obscured in the earlier account, but neither establishes lifelong physical learning with retention.

change_log.change: Qualified the roadmap, DeepMind report and π0.7 evidence according to source type and access.
change_log.reason: An abstract-only roadmap, developer-reported adaptation figures and a partially extracted preprint support different levels of inference.

change_log.change: Bounded the expected impact to the demonstrated operating range and made broader deployment consequences conditional.
change_log.reason: Learning efficiency does not independently establish perception, dexterity, safety, reliability or economic adoption.

change_log.change: Retained single-demonstration acquisition and cross-body transfer as stricter proposals while removing unsupported historical attribution.
change_log.reason: Their historical provenance is absent, and execution on one second body cannot establish arbitrary-body transfer.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed completion tests to cover prior exposure, total learning cost, retention, memory rules, replication and operating boundaries.
change_log.reason: These details make the proposed capability assessable without presenting chosen thresholds as consensus standards or finite tests as universal proof.

unresolved_issues: No supplied freshness search establishes whether other work had demonstrated the complete capability by 1 November 2026.
Task count, correction accounting, success thresholds, acceptable retention loss, trial counts and practical resource limits remain to be specified for the proposed demonstration.
The permitted memory and replay mechanisms require an operational definition consistent with the proposed prohibition on offline replay of original demonstrations.
Auditing genuine task novelty remains difficult when pretraining data are broad or incompletely disclosed.
The provenance of the claimed historical single-demonstration and arbitrary-body wording is not supplied; those requirements are preserved only as proposed extensions.
The feasible range of embodiments and tasks for stronger transfer claims remains undefined.
ROB-01 and the other related entries are supplied only as titles, limiting exact catalog overlap assessment.

The roadmap's full text was unavailable, π0.7's extraction ends during Appendix A-G, and videos were not inspected in the supplied review. These limits prevent exhaustive conclusions about their contents.
DeepMind's adaptation figures remain developer reports without independent verification in the supplied material.

brief.title: Robots that keep learning without forgetting
possible: When a kitchen, warehouse or laboratory changes its procedures, people could teach a robot the new job through a few instructions or corrections. The robot would keep its earlier skills and combine them to do a job it had never been shown from start to finish, even in a different room.
why: Teaching physical work could become part of everyday work. Each new lesson would add to the robot’s abilities while preserving the effort spent teaching it before. Workers could adapt robots to changing procedures with less need for large training campaigns.

sources.showed: This preprint reports laundry folding on a robot never trained on that task, new combinations of existing skills, and learning longer jobs from episodes coached through language.
sources.quote: our approach enables learning from mixed-quality data and non-standard data sources without hurting the model performance, and diverse data boosts the model performance when detailed context information is provided during training.
sources.cited_for: It supports skill reuse across robot bodies and learning from language coaching.
sources.not_established: It does not establish learning a sequence of new physical tasks while retaining earlier skills.

sources.showed: DeepMind reports adapting its robot model to unfamiliar bodies with paired arms through additional training.
sources.quote: We can now adapt to new bi-arm robot embodiments with just a few hours of adaptation time
sources.cited_for: It supports rapid adaptation to different robot bodies.
sources.not_established: These developer-reported results do not establish transfer without further training or cumulative learning without forgetting.

sources.showed: Their LEGION system learned successive tasks while preserving knowledge in simulation. A physical robot then reused and combined the learned skills without updating its model.
sources.quote: Furthermore, our agent can tackle challenging real-world long-horizon tasks by combining and reapplying its acquired knowledge from the original tasks stream.
sources.cited_for: It supports preserving knowledge through successive tasks and combining learned skills for physical work.
sources.not_established: The physical robot did not acquire new tasks through limited instruction during deployment.

sources.showed: Their research roadmap identifies continued learning and safe deployment as long-term challenges, alongside transferring algorithms between robot platforms.
sources.cited_for: It explains why continued learning and safe operation remain connected research challenges.
sources.not_established: A roadmap does not demonstrate a robot that learns safely while retaining and combining its skills.

shown: Yuan Meng and colleagues’ LEGION system learned a sequence of ten tasks in simulation while preserving knowledge. A physical robot then combined those skills for jobs such as cleaning a table, but its model stayed fixed during physical use.

Physical Intelligence’s preprint reports skill transfer between robot bodies and learning longer jobs through language coaching. These results demonstrate useful parts of the capability; they do not establish continued physical learning together with measured retention and reuse in a new setting.
missing: A deployed robot has yet to demonstrate the full combination of learning new tasks from sparse instruction, retaining old ones and reusing them elsewhere.
Learning costs must include exploration, resets, human help and computation, with competent and safe behavior maintained during updates.
Skills must remain reliable when objects, surroundings and preceding actions change.

milestones.label: New physical tasks learned beyond starting abilities
milestones.explanation: A robot would have to learn a predeclared task sequence excluded from its documented training history, with performance measured before teaching. This would distinguish new learning from existing ability.

milestones.label: Learning within a small, fully counted teaching budget
milestones.explanation: Each task would have to use only tens of corrections, with their duration and all interaction, exploration, resets, assistance, computation and elapsed time counted. This would reveal the full cost of teaching.

milestones.label: Earlier skills survive subsequent learning
milestones.explanation: Every earlier task would have to pass declared retention tests after subsequent learning and at the end, without retraining. Individual and combined results would expose forgetting hidden by averages.

milestones.label: Learned skills combine into a new-room job
milestones.explanation: A robot would have to combine acquired skills in a new room without a complete job demonstration or offline replay of original demonstrations. Declared setup aids and permitted memory would clarify this stricter test.

milestones.label: Repeated learning succeeds within stated practical boundaries
milestones.explanation: Repeated runs with declared task orders would have to report variation, failures, interventions and safety events, with replication records and operating limits. This would establish reliability within tested boundaries.

milestones.label: A skill transfers after a single demonstration
milestones.explanation: A skill learned from a single demonstration would have to work on a different robot without further training, with calibration and setup changes declared. This would establish transfer to that tested body.

uncertain: Broad or undisclosed training data make it difficult to tell whether a task is genuinely new to a robot.
Success thresholds, acceptable forgetting and practical limits on teaching effort still need to be defined.
Permitted memory and replay need clear rules, as does the range of robot bodies and physically feasible tasks used to judge transfer.

page.title: Lifelong learning for robot manipulation
page.definition: A physical robot acquires manipulation tasks sequentially during deployment, retains earlier task performance, and combines acquired motor skills to complete an undemonstrated task in a new environment. Manipulation means acting on objects by grasping, moving or using them.

goal.need: LIBERO supplies 50 demonstrations for each of 130 simulated manipulation tasks. LEGION trains for 1 million steps on each of 10 simulated tasks. The goal is to reuse acquired knowledge as tasks change while preserving earlier performance, so that learning another task does not discard previous training. These are experimental training budgets, not measured deployment costs.

statements.quote: enable systems to learn from experience on the fly
statements.context: The programme describes the purpose of developing new machine-learning mechanisms.

statements.body: Billard and colleagues, authors of A roadmap for AI in robotics
statements.quote: to design robots capable of lifelong learning, while guaranteeing safe deployment and usage, and sustainable computational costs.
statements.context: The authors identify this as a primary long-term challenge.

statements.quote: They lack the ability to truly learn for themselves or adapt to unpredictable environments.
statements.context: The passage refers to robots programmed or teleoperated for narrow, repetitive task sequences.

completion.title: One robot learns sequential tasks, retains them and composes them in an unseen environment.
completion.criterion: One physical manipulator must acquire new tasks through a deployment-time sequence, with L2M sample efficiency SE > 1 against single-task learners and performance maintenance PM ≥ 0 on earlier tasks. After those updates, it must complete an undemonstrated combination of the newly acquired skills in an environment absent from instruction. SE compares saturated performance and experiences needed to reach it; PM is the mean change in earlier-task performance during subsequent learning. Replay is permitted. No universal task count, instruction budget or trial count is specified.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis of published component criteria; no external integrated completion test found.
completion.basis: DARPA L2M programme and metrics documents, the robotics roadmap, LIBERO, and web searches for robotics standards and competitions yielded no integrated physical acquisition–retention–composition pass test or universal instruction budget. L2M supplies SE > 1 and PM ≥ 0 as component interpretations. Their conjunction with composition in an unseen environment is an Atlas synthesis.

milestones.title: A simulated robot learns a task stream with mean forgetting no greater than zero.
milestones.criterion: For a simulated manipulation-task stream, require F ≤ 0, where F is the mean, over all but the final task, of success immediately after learning that task minus success after the entire stream. Improvements can offset losses in this aggregate. On 5 February 2025, LEGION reported F = 0.0 and final mean success 0.84 across 10 simulated tasks trained for 1 million steps each. Its physical deployment froze the learned parameters.
milestones.set_by: The signed forgetting convention used in lifelong learning, defined in LEGION, Methods: Forgetting.
milestones.threshold_quote: When F > 0 represents that the agent may have lost knowledge of prior tasks.

milestones.title: A physical robot scores 7/7 on the held-out Toast a Bagel composition task.
milestones.criterion: Complete the physical Toast a Bagel protocol for all 7 rubric points: open the oven, insert the bagel, close the oven, turn the knob, retrieve a plate, retrieve the toast and plate it. Stepwise language coaching is allowed; the complete task has no robot-training episodes. The π0.7 preprint of 24 April 2026 reports coached execution and subsequent training of autonomous high-level policies from coaching episodes. These results are not peer reviewed and do not test earlier-task retention.
milestones.set_by: Physical Intelligence, π0.7, Appendix A-G; this published task endpoint applies specifically to Toast a Bagel.
milestones.threshold_quote: Maximum score: 7 (open oven; insert bagel; close oven; turn knob; retrieve plate; retrieve toast; place on plate).

milestones.title: A physical robot learns manipulation tasks with L2M sample efficiency greater than 1.
milestones.criterion: On physical manipulation tasks with saturated learning curves, require mean L2M sample efficiency SE > 1. For each task, SE = (learner saturation / single-task-expert saturation) × (expert experiences to saturation / learner experiences to saturation). On 30 July 2026, Google DeepMind reported adaptation to new paired-arm robots in a few hours, typically using fewer than 200 examples. This developer report is not peer reviewed and does not supply the matched learning curves needed to establish SE > 1.
milestones.set_by: Johns Hopkins APL L2M evaluation team, Lifelong Learning Metrics, section 3.4.5; its domain-agnostic criterion is applied here to physical manipulation.
milestones.threshold_quote: L2 agent demonstrates better performance than the Single Task Expert;

milestones.title: A physical robot retains sequentially acquired tasks with mean performance maintenance of at least 0.
milestones.criterion: After a physical robot acquires new tasks sequentially, require L2M PM ≥ 0: average the changes in earlier-task performance relative to each task's most recent post-learning evaluation, excluding that immediate evaluation. Evaluation blocks exercise all previously learned tasks. The LifelongVLA preprint of 21 July 2026 reports five xArm tasks, 50 training episodes per task and 50 evaluation episodes per seen task after each stage, with final success above 80% on every task. Those final rates alone do not establish PM ≥ 0; the result is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Johns Hopkins APL L2M evaluation team, Lifelong Learning Metrics, section 3.4.1; its domain-agnostic criterion is applied here to physical manipulation.
milestones.threshold_quote: PM = 0: No forgetting; no additional learning.

not_found: No external integrated completion criterion or universal instruction budget was found in the programme documents, roadmap, benchmarks and standards or competition searches.
No opened study establishes acquisition efficiency, retention and subsequent composition of the newly acquired skills in an unseen environment in the same physical learning sequence.
The opened π0.7 text does not state evaluation episode counts for the coached Toast a Bagel experiment.
The opened LifelongVLA text does not provide the stagewise physical success values needed to calculate L2M performance maintenance.
The published Neural Networks article on domain-agnostic lifelong-learning evaluation could not be opened; the separate L2M metrics document was accessible.
